items.stem: What is the molar mass of water?
items.answer: 18.02 g mol⁻¹

items.stem: Sana writes: "The molar mass of magnesium is 24.31 g." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Molar mass has units of g mol⁻¹; 24.31 g is the mass of one mole.
items.markingKey: Molar mass has units of g mol⁻¹; 24.31 g is the mass of one mole. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why the mole is needed in chemistry.
items.answer: Atoms and molecules are far too small to count individually; the mole links a countable mass of substance to a fixed number of particles (6.02 × 10²³), allowing reacting quantities to be calculated from equations.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Atoms and molecules are far too small to count individually; the mole links a countable mass of substance to a fixed number of particles (6.02 × 10²³), allowing reacting quantities to be calculated from equations. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Calculate the number of formula units (or molecules) in 19.62 g of calcium phosphate, Ca₃(PO₄)₂.
Calculate the number of formula units (or molecules) in 10.16 g of aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃.

A student heated magnesium ribbon in a lidded crucible to find the empirical formula of magnesium oxide. A balance reading to ±0.01 g was used.

mass of crucible + lid / g | 29.11
mass of crucible + lid + Mg / g | 29.28
mass of crucible + lid + product / g | 29.38

(a) Calculate the mass of magnesium used and the mass of oxygen that reacted. [2]
(b) Determine the mole ratio Mg : O and comment on the result. [2]
(c) Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the mass of magnesium. [2]
(d) Suggest one reason why the ratio obtained is lower than expected, and one improvement. [1]
(e) Suggest how the percentage uncertainty in the mass of magnesium could be reduced. [1]
items.answer: (a) Mg 0.17 g; O 0.10 g (b) 1 : 0.89 (expected 1 : 1) (c) 12 % (d) Magnesium not fully oxidised (or some reacted with nitrogen / MgO smoke escaped when the lid was lifted); heat to constant mass and lift the lid only briefly. (e) Use a larger mass of magnesium (or a balance with higher resolution, ±0.001 g).
items.markingKey: (a) [2] 0.17 g and 0.10 g (A1 A1). (b) [2] n(Mg) = 0.0070, n(O) = 0.0063 (M1); ratio 1 : 0.89, lower than 1 : 1 expected (A1). (c) [2] two readings: ±0.02 g (M1); 0.02/0.17 × 100 = 12 % (A1). (d) [1] Valid cause (1). (e) [1] Larger mass / more precise balance (1).

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "The redefinition of the mole in 2019 (fixing NA exactly) was a significant improvement."
items.answer: Conceptually cleaner and more stable at the highest precision, though invisible in school-level calculations (NOS: measurement standards evolve).
items.markingKey: Arguments for: NA is now exact, independent of an artefact or a ¹²C mass measurement; consistent with the other SI base units defined by constants. Arguments against: makes no practical difference to everyday calculations; molar mass of ¹²C is no longer exactly 12 g mol⁻¹. Supported judgement: Conceptually cleaner and more stable at the highest precision, though invisible in school-level calculations (NOS: measurement standards evolve).

items.stem: A tablet contains 500 mg of paracetamol, C₈H₉NO₂. (a) Calculate the molar mass of paracetamol. (b) Calculate the number of paracetamol molecules in one tablet. (c) Calculate the total number of carbon atoms in the paracetamol in one tablet.
Outline the meaning of the term "amount of substance".
items.answer: The quantity, measured in moles, that is proportional to the number of specified particles in a sample

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The number of particles per mole of substance, 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹"?
items.answer: Avogadro constant (NA)

items.stem: Explain the difference between molar mass and relative molecular mass.
items.answer: Relative molecular mass is a dimensionless ratio (relative to 1/12 of ¹²C); molar mass is the mass of one mole and has units g mol⁻¹ – numerically equal.
items.markingKey: Relative molecular mass is a dimensionless ratio (relative to 1/12 of ¹²C); molar mass is the mass of one mole and has units g mol⁻¹ – numerically equal. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Deduce, showing your working, whether 12.9 g of calcium hydroxide (Ca(OH)₂) or 12.9 g of water (H₂O) contains more atoms.
items.answer: water (1.29 × 10²⁴ atoms vs 5.24 × 10²³)

items.stem: Define the term "percentage composition by mass".
items.answer: The mass of each element in a compound expressed as a percentage of the total mass

items.stem: Explain why the empirical formula alone cannot identify a compound.
items.answer: Many different compounds share the same simplest ratio (e.g. CH₂O for methanal, ethanoic acid and glucose); the molar mass is needed to find the molecular formula, and even then isomers may exist.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Many different compounds share the same simplest ratio (e.g. CH₂O for methanal, ethanoic acid and glucose); the molar mass is needed to find the molecular formula, and even then isomers may exist. items.stem: A student claims: "The empirical formula of hydrogen peroxide, H₂O₂, is H₂O." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Dividing by the common factor 2 gives HO; H₂O is a different compound (water).
items.markingKey: Dividing by the common factor 2 gives HO; H₂O is a different compound (water). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Analysis of a sample shows it contains iron 69.9 %, oxygen 30.1 %. What is the empirical formula?
items.answer: Fe₂O₃
items.markingKey: B. Divide each % by Ar, then by the smallest: ratio 1.00 : 1.50 → Fe₂O₃.

items.stem: Analysis of a sample shows it contains carbon 82.6 %, hydrogen 17.4 %. Determine the empirical formula.
items.answer: C₂H₅
items.markingKey: n = %/Ar: C 6.878, H 17.228 (M1); divide by smallest: 1.00 : 2.50; multiply by 2 (M1); C₂H₅ (A1).

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Combustion analysis is a reliable method for determining the empirical formula of an organic compound."
items.answer: Reliable for C and H when combustion is complete and samples pure, but must be combined with mass spectrometry and spectroscopy for full identification.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: precise masses of CO₂ and H₂O give C and H directly; automated CHN analysers are fast and need milligram samples. Arguments against: incomplete combustion or impurities give wrong ratios; oxygen is found only by difference, accumulating errors; it gives no information on structure or isomers. Supported judgement: Reliable for C and H when combustion is complete and samples pure, but must be combined with mass spectrometry and spectroscopy for full identification.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "molecular formula"?
options: The volume occupied by one mole of any ideal gas at a stated temperature and pressure; 22.7 dm³ mol⁻¹ at STP (273 K, 100 kPa)
The addition of solvent to a solution, which lowers its concentration while the amount of solute stays the same
The actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule of a compound; a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula
A temperature of 273 K (0 °C) and a pressure of 100 kPa
items.answer: The actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule of a compound; a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula
items.markingKey: C. "molecular formula" is the actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule of a compound; a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula.

items.stem: A compound has the empirical formula CH₂O and molar mass 180 g mol⁻¹. How many carbon atoms are in one molecule?
Explain the difference between molecular formula and empirical formula.
items.answer: The empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms; the molecular formula gives the actual number of each atom in a molecule and is n × the empirical formula.
items.markingKey: The empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms; the molecular formula gives the actual number of each atom in a molecule and is n × the empirical formula. items.stem: Briefly explain why the total volume of solution, not the volume of water added, is used in concentration calculations.
items.answer: Concentration is amount per unit volume of solution; dissolving a solute changes the volume, so a solution is made up to the mark in a volumetric flask.

items.answer: The final solution volume is not exactly 1.00 dm³; the solid should be dissolved and made up to 1.00 dm³ of solution.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Expressing the concentration of pollutants in parts per million (ppm) is more useful to the public than mol dm⁻³."
items.answer: ppm suits communication and regulation; mol dm⁻³ is essential for chemical calculations – the choice depends on the audience.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: ppm is intuitive and used in legal limits; convenient for very small concentrations. items.stem: A standard solution was made by dissolving 1.278 g of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, in water and making up to 250.0 cm³. 25.0 cm³ of this solution was diluted to 100.0 cm³ (solution B); then 10.0 cm³ of B was diluted to 100.0 cm³ (solution C). (a) Calculate the concentration of the original solution. (b) Calculate the concentration of solution C in mol dm⁻³ and in mg dm⁻³. (c) State one advantage of serial dilution over weighing a tiny mass directly.
items.answer: (a) 0.0284 mol dm⁻³; (b) 7.09 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ = 128 mg dm⁻³
items.markingKey: (a) n = 1.278/180.18 = 0.00709 mol; c = 0.0284 mol dm⁻³ (M1 A1). (b) dilution factors 4 and 10 (M1); c(C) = 7.09 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ (A1); × 180.18 × 1000 = 128 mg dm⁻³ (A1). (c) The percentage uncertainty in weighing a very small mass would be very large (R1).

items.stem: Explain the difference between g dm⁻³ and mol dm⁻³.

items.stem: Define the term "Avogadro's law".
items.answer: Equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of particles

items.stem: Why do 1 mol of H₂ and 1 mol of CO₂ occupy the same volume at STP?
options: Particle volume is negligible compared with the volume of the gas.
They have the same intermolecular forces.
items.answer: Particle volume is negligible compared with the volume of the gas.
items.markingKey: A. Ideal-gas behaviour.

items.stem: Distinguish between Avogadro's law and the molar volume.
items.answer: Avogadro's law states equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of particles at the same T and p; the molar volume is the specific volume of one mole under stated conditions (22.7 dm³ at STP).
items.markingKey: Avogadro's law states equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of particles at the same T and p; the molar volume is the specific volume of one mole under stated conditions (22.7 dm³ at STP). items.stem: Consider the reaction C₂H₄(g) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l). Calculate the volume of C₂H₄ that reacts with or is produced from 25.0 cm³ of O₂, all volumes measured at the same temperature and pressure.
items.answer: 8.33 cm³
items.markingKey: Volume ratio = mole ratio O₂ : C₂H₄ = 3 : 1 (M1); V = 25.0 × 1/3 = 8.33 cm³ (A1).

items.stem: Calculate the mass of 44.2 dm³ of propane, C₃H₈, measured at STP.

25.0 cm³ of ethane is exploded with 175 cm³ of oxygen: 2C₂H₆(g) + 7O₂(g) → 4CO₂(g) + 6H₂O(l). After cooling to the original room temperature and pressure, water is a liquid. (a) Determine the volume of each gas remaining. (b) Determine the total gas volume. (c) State and explain how the volume would change if the mixture were then passed through aqueous sodium hydroxide.
items.answer: (a) CO₂ 50.0 cm³, O₂ 87.5 cm³; (b) 138 cm³; (c) falls to 87.5 cm³ as CO₂ is absorbed

items.stem: Explain why, according to Avogadro's law, equal volumes of hydrogen and carbon dioxide at the same temperature and pressure contain the same number of molecules.
items.answer: In an ideal gas the volume of the particles themselves is negligible and there are no intermolecular forces, so the volume depends only on the number of particles, T and p, not on their identity or size.

items.stem: "One mole of liquid water occupies 22.7 dm³ at STP." Explain the flaw in this statement.

items.stem: "Avogadro's law applies to all gases under all conditions." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: It is an ideal-gas law – an excellent approximation at low pressure and high temperature but not exact for real gases.

Arguments against: real gases deviate at high pressure and low temperature; polar or large molecules (e.g. NH₃, CO₂) deviate more due to intermolecular forces and particle volume. Supported judgement: It is an ideal-gas law – an excellent approximation at low pressure and high temperature but not exact for real gases. items.stem: Distinguish between mol dm⁻³ and g dm⁻³.
items.answer: mol dm⁻³ gives the amount of solute per dm³; g dm⁻³ gives its mass per dm³; they are related by the molar mass (g dm⁻³ = mol dm⁻³ × M).
items.markingKey: mol dm⁻³ gives the amount of solute per dm³; g dm⁻³ gives its mass per dm³; they are related by the molar mass (g dm⁻³ = mol dm⁻³ × M). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why an ionic compound such as sodium chloride has only an empirical formula and no molecular formula.
items.answer: It is a giant lattice of ions with no discrete molecules; the formula NaCl represents only the simplest ratio of ions.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It is a giant lattice of ions with no discrete molecules; the formula NaCl represents only the simplest ratio of ions. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: At constant T and p, 1 volume of a gaseous element reacts with 3 volumes of hydrogen to give 2 volumes of a single product. Which element?
items.answer: nitrogen
items.markingKey: D. N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃.

items.stem: Distinguish between the number of molecules and the number of atoms in a sample.
items.answer: Number of molecules = n × NA; number of atoms = n × NA × atoms per molecule.
items.markingKey: Number of molecules = n × NA; number of atoms = n × NA × atoms per molecule. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Chloé checked the mass of a weighing boat containing solute in repeated weighings. The repeated readings of the mass of solute were 1.329, 1.298, 1.328 g. Calculate the mean and its absolute uncertainty.
items.markingKey: Mean = 1.318 g (A1); uncertainty = half the range = (1.329 − 1.298)/2 = 0.015 g (A1).

items.stem: Lukas heated 2.473 g of tin in a crucible until it had all reacted with oxygen. The mass of tin oxide formed was 3.140 g. Determine the empirical formula of the oxide.
items.answer: SnO₂

items.stem:
A student heated magnesium ribbon in a lidded crucible to find the empirical formula of magnesium oxide. A balance reading to ±0.01 g was used.

mass of crucible + lid / g | 27.88
mass of crucible + lid + Mg / g | 28.15
mass of crucible + lid + product / g | 28.30

(a) Calculate the mass of magnesium used and the mass of oxygen that reacted. [2]
(b) Determine the mole ratio Mg : O and comment on the result. [2]
(c) Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the mass of magnesium. [2]
(d) Suggest one reason why the ratio obtained is lower than expected, and one improvement. [1]
(e) Suggest how the percentage uncertainty in the mass of magnesium could be reduced. [1]
items.answer: (a) Mg 0.27 g; O 0.15 g (b) 1 : 0.84 (expected 1 : 1) (c) 7 % (d) Magnesium not fully oxidised (or some reacted with nitrogen / MgO smoke escaped when the lid was lifted); heat to constant mass and lift the lid only briefly. (e) Use a larger mass of magnesium (or a balance with higher resolution, ±0.001 g).
items.markingKey: (a) [2] 0.27 g and 0.15 g (A1 A1). (b) [2] n(Mg) = 0.0111, n(O) = 0.0094 (M1); ratio 1 : 0.84, lower than 1 : 1 expected (A1). (c) [2] two readings: ±0.02 g (M1); 0.02/0.27 × 100 = 7 % (A1). (d) [1] Valid cause (1). (e) [1] Larger mass / more precise balance (1).

items.stem: Leila writes: "One mole of oxygen gas contains 6.02 × 10²³ oxygen atoms." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Oxygen gas is O₂: one mole contains 6.02 × 10²³ molecules and 1.20 × 10²⁴ atoms.
items.markingKey: Oxygen gas is O₂: one mole contains 6.02 × 10²³ molecules and 1.20 × 10²⁴ atoms. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Nia dissolves 14.24 g of potassium iodide, KI, in water and makes the solution up to 500.0 cm³. Calculate the concentration in mol dm⁻³.
items.answer: 0.172 mol dm⁻³

items.stem: Determine the mass of hydrogen in 50.0 g of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆.
Consider the reaction 2NO(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO₂(g). Calculate the volume of NO that reacts with or is produced from 20.0 cm³ of NO₂, all volumes measured at the same temperature and pressure.
items.answer: 20.0 cm³
items.markingKey: Volume ratio = mole ratio NO₂ : NO = 2 : 2 (M1); V = 20.0 × 2/2 = 20.0 cm³ (A1).

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The redefinition of the mole in 2019 (fixing NA exactly) was a significant improvement."
items.answer: Conceptually cleaner and more stable at the highest precision, though invisible in school-level calculations (NOS: measurement standards evolve).
items.markingKey: Arguments for: NA is now exact, independent of an artefact or a ¹²C mass measurement; consistent with the other SI base units defined by constants. Arguments against: makes no practical difference to everyday calculations; molar mass of ¹²C is no longer exactly 12 g mol⁻¹. Supported judgement: Conceptually cleaner and more stable at the highest precision, though invisible in school-level calculations (NOS: measurement standards evolve).

items.stem: A standard solution was made by dissolving 2.352 g of potassium hydrogen phthalate, C₈H₅KO₄, in water and making up to 250.0 cm³. 20.0 cm³ of this solution was diluted to 250.0 cm³ (solution B); then 5.0 cm³ of B was diluted to 100.0 cm³ (solution C). (a) Calculate the concentration of the original solution. (b) Calculate the concentration of solution C in mol dm⁻³ and in mg dm⁻³. (c) State one advantage of serial dilution over weighing a tiny mass directly.
items.answer: (a) 0.0461 mol dm⁻³; (b) 1.84 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ = 37.6 mg dm⁻³
items.markingKey: (a) n = 2.352/204.23 = 0.0115 mol; c = 0.0461 mol dm⁻³ (M1 A1). (b) dilution factors 12.5 and 20 (M1); c(C) = 1.84 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ (A1); × 204.23 × 1000 = 37.6 mg dm⁻³ (A1). (c) The percentage uncertainty in weighing a very small mass would be very large (R1).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Combustion analysis is a reliable method for determining the empirical formula of an organic compound."
items.answer: Reliable for C and H when combustion is complete and samples pure, but must be combined with mass spectrometry and spectroscopy for full identification.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: precise masses of CO₂ and H₂O give C and H directly; automated CHN analysers are fast and need milligram samples. Arguments against: incomplete combustion or impurities give wrong ratios; oxygen is found only by difference, accumulating errors; it gives no information on structure or isomers. Supported judgement: Reliable for C and H when combustion is complete and samples pure, but must be combined with mass spectrometry and spectroscopy for full identification. Markbands (6 marks): IB-style extended response: 9-12 – accurate chemistry throughout, correct terminology, equations/data used to support each point, balanced evaluation and a justified conclusion; 5-8 – mostly accurate, some support, limited evaluation; 1-4 – fragmentary, largely descriptive.

items.stem: 30.0 cm³ of ethene is exploded with 108 cm³ of oxygen: C₂H₄(g) + 3O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l). After cooling to the original room temperature and pressure, water is a liquid. (a) Determine the volume of each gas remaining. (b) Determine the total gas volume. (c) State and explain how the volume would change if the mixture were then passed through aqueous sodium hydroxide.
items.answer: (a) CO₂ 60.0 cm³, O₂ 18.0 cm³; (b) 78.0 cm³; (c) falls to 18.0 cm³ as CO₂ is absorbed
items.markingKey: (a) O₂ used = 30.0 × 3/1 = 90.0 cm³ (M1); O₂ left 18.0 cm³ (A1); CO₂ = 60.0 cm³ (A1). (b) 78.0 cm³ (A1). (c) NaOH (an alkali) absorbs the acidic CO₂, leaving 18.0 cm³ O₂ (R1).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "mole"?
options: A solution whose concentration is known accurately
The addition of solvent to a solution, which lowers its concentration while the amount of solute stays the same
The SI unit of amount of substance; one mole contains exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ elementary entities
Equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of particles
items.answer: The SI unit of amount of substance; one mole contains exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ elementary entities
items.markingKey: C. "mole" is the SI unit of amount of substance; one mole contains exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ elementary entities.

items.stem: Which piece of glassware should be used to prepare 250.0 cm³ of a standard solution?
items.answer: a volumetric flask
items.markingKey: D. Volumetric flasks have the smallest uncertainty for a fixed volume.

items.stem: A ratio of atoms in a calculation comes out as C 1 : H 2.5. What is the empirical formula?
items.answer: C₂H₅
items.markingKey: C₂H₅. Multiply by 2 to obtain whole numbers.

items.stem: Explain the difference between Avogadro's law and the molar volume.
items.answer: Avogadro's law states equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of particles at the same T and p; the molar volume is the specific volume of one mole under stated conditions (22.7 dm³ at STP).
items.markingKey: Avogadro's law states equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of particles at the same T and p; the molar volume is the specific volume of one mole under stated conditions (22.7 dm³ at STP). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "One mole of oxygen gas contains 6.02 × 10²³ oxygen atoms." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Oxygen gas is O₂: one mole contains 6.02 × 10²³ molecules and 1.20 × 10²⁴ atoms.
items.markingKey: Oxygen gas is O₂: one mole contains 6.02 × 10²³ molecules and 1.20 × 10²⁴ atoms. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why a solid should be dissolved in a beaker and the washings transferred to the volumetric flask when making a standard solution.
items.answer: This ensures all the solute is dissolved and transferred, so the amount in the flask is exactly the amount weighed; rinsing transfers traces left on the glassware.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: This ensures all the solute is dissolved and transferred, so the amount in the flask is exactly the amount weighed; rinsing transfers traces left on the glassware. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Arjun writes: "The empirical formula of hydrogen peroxide, H₂O₂, is H₂O." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Dividing by the common factor 2 gives HO; H₂O is a different compound (water).
items.markingKey: Dividing by the common factor 2 gives HO; H₂O is a different compound (water). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: 20 cm³ of methane is burned completely in excess oxygen. What volume of CO₂ forms at the same T and p?
items.answer: 20 cm³
items.markingKey: B. CH₄ : CO₂ = 1 : 1.

items.stem: Which sample contains 1.20 × 10²⁴ atoms? (NA = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)
items.answer: 1.00 mol of O₂
items.markingKey: D. atoms = n × atoms per molecule × NA = 1.00 × 2 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.20 × 10²⁴.

items.stem: Freya writes: "Diluting 10 cm³ of a solution to 100 cm³ halves its concentration." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: A tenfold increase in volume reduces the concentration by a factor of 10.
items.markingKey: A tenfold increase in volume reduces the concentration by a factor of 10. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Sofia heated 1.137 g of lead in a crucible until it had all reacted with oxygen. The mass of lead oxide formed was 1.225 g. Determine the empirical formula of the oxide.
items.answer: PbO

items.stem: Calculate the mass of 33.1 dm³ of chlorine, Cl₂, measured at STP.
A sample of ammonium nitrate contains 7.23 × 10²² molecules (formula units). Calculate its mass.
A solution of potassium hydrogen phthalate has a concentration of 0.248 mol dm⁻³. Calculate its concentration in g dm⁻³.
items.answer: 50.6 g dm⁻³

items.stem: A compound contains 72.2 % magnesium, 27.8 % nitrogen by mass. Its molar mass is 100.9 g mol⁻¹. Determine its empirical and molecular formulae.
items.answer: EF Mg₃N₂; MF Mg₃N₂

items.stem: Calculate the volume, at STP, occupied by 34.6 g of ammonia, NH₃.
items.answer: 46.1 dm³

items.stem: A 4.951 g sample of hydrated barium chloride, BaCl₂·xH₂O, was heated to constant mass. The anhydrous residue had a mass of 4.221 g. (a) Calculate the amount of anhydrous salt and of water. (b) Determine x. (c) Explain why the sample was heated to constant mass.
items.markingKey: (a) n(salt) = 4.221/208.23 = 0.0203 mol; n(H₂O) = 0.730/18.02 = 0.0405 mol (M1 M1). (b) ratio 2.00 → x = 2 (A1). (c) to ensure all water of crystallisation is removed (R1).

items.stem: "Expressing the concentration of pollutants in parts per million (ppm) is more useful to the public than mol dm⁻³." Discuss.
items.answer: ppm suits communication and regulation; mol dm⁻³ is essential for chemical calculations – the choice depends on the audience.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: ppm is intuitive and used in legal limits; convenient for very small concentrations. Arguments against: mol dm⁻³ is needed for stoichiometric and toxicological calculations; ppm can be ambiguous (mass/mass or volume/volume). Supported judgement: ppm suits communication and regulation; mol dm⁻³ is essential for chemical calculations – the choice depends on the audience. items.stem: A 0.404 g sample of an organic compound containing carbon and hydrogen only was burned completely in excess oxygen, forming 1.245 g of carbon dioxide and 0.573 g of water. Determine the empirical formula of the compound, showing all working.
items.answer: C₄H₉

items.stem: "Avogadro's law applies to all gases under all conditions." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: It is an ideal-gas law – an excellent approximation at low pressure and high temperature but not exact for real gases.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: works well for most gases at ordinary T and p; basis of molar volume calculations. Arguments against: real gases deviate at high pressure and low temperature; polar or large molecules (e.g. NH₃, CO₂) deviate more due to intermolecular forces and particle volume. Supported judgement: It is an ideal-gas law – an excellent approximation at low pressure and high temperature but not exact for real gases.
